catalog_quote: 1.3 Tones. There are six live tones: two level (55, 33), two rising (35, 13), one falling (31) and the slight tone (atonality) 'ø'. The slight tone 'ø' appears only in some prefixes. The dead tones have pitch shapes 55, 33, 31. Dead tones occur with either lax or tense vowel syllables. Tones are instable in Bugan, a part of the lexicon can be pronounced with either of two tones ... (p. 141) ... 2.1.2.2. Derived words. There are two main types of derivation: prefix + head, head + suffix. All prefixes are pronounced with tone, but a few of them are pronounced with the slight tone. (p. 144)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Bugan is described as a lexical-tone language (five full tones on open syllables, three on checked syllables). The source makes no statement about word stress or accent; the only prominence-related fact is that a toneless 'slight tone' (i.e. a neutral/atonic, reduced syllable) is restricted to a subset of prefixal first syllables (pə⁰-, tə⁰-, lə⁰-, tse⁰-), while roots/main syllables always bear a full tone — consistent with the Austroasiatic weak-presyllable + full main-syllable word shape, but not stated as a stress rule by the author.
new_statements.exceptions: Most prefixes carry a full lexical tone (pə⁵⁵-, te⁵⁵-, na³³-, mu³³-, pu⁵⁵- etc.); only 'a few' take the slight (neutral) tone. Tones are unstable (many words have two alternative tones) and undergo progressive sandhi in context.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level citation forms (monosyllables and prefix+root disyllables) from the Nala-area variety, 1994 fieldwork; tone values in context differ from citation values (sandhi).
new_statements.identity_note: Li 1996 (and Li & Luo 2015) describe the Nala-area variety of Guangnan County (autonym pə⁵⁵kan³³; six tones incl. neutral). Li Yunbing 2005 describes the Manlong 曼龙 variety of Xichou County (autonym pu⁵⁵qeŋ⁴⁴; four tones 55/44/24/31). Both fall under glottocode buga1247 (no dialect-level codes in Glottolog); Li 1996 claims 'There is no variation in the Bugan language', Hsiu 2016 reports speakers acknowledge some internal variation.

tone_statements.quote: Words with final stops are few; these words appear only with tone 55, 33, 31 (only two with the tone 33 in my record). … There are six live tones: two levels (55, 33), two risings (35, 13), one falling (31) and the slight tone (atonality) 'o'. The slight tone 'o' appears only in some prefixes. The dead tones have pitch shapes 55, 33, 31. Dead tones occur with either lax vowel syllables or tense vowel syllables. Tones are shaky in Bugan, part of words can be pronounced with two tones … Tonal change is common in context, and many cases are progressive assimilation
tone_statements.summary: Six tones on live syllables: level 55, 33, rising 35, 13, falling 31 and a toneless 'slight tone' on some prefixes; stop-final syllables only 55, 33, 31; many words have two tones; tone sandhi.
